clinicalPearls: Results from impaired function of the vagus or recurrent laryngeal nerve, so establishing the cause along the whole nerve course is essential
Unilateral paralysis typically causes a breathy, weak voice with a poor cough and aspiration risk from incomplete glottic closure
Bilateral paralysis, with both folds near the midline, threatens the airway and can present with stridor and dyspnoea, often with a surprisingly good voice
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve's long intrathoracic course makes it vulnerable to mediastinal and aortic pathology
Iatrogenic injury, especially after thyroid, parathyroid, anterior cervical spine, or cardiothoracic surgery, is a leading cause
Unilateral cases are managed with voice therapy and, where compensation is inadequate, injection augmentation or medialisation thyroplasty
Bilateral paralysis may require a temporary tracheostomy for the airway, with later procedures to enlarge the glottis balanced against voice
reference.pathophysiology: Vocal fold paralysis arises from interruption of the motor supply to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles anywhere along the vagus nerve and its recurrent laryngeal branch, from the brainstem nucleus to the muscle. Because the recurrent laryngeal nerve loops into the thorax, particularly on the left around the aortic arch, lesions in the neck, chest, or skull base can all be responsible; common mechanisms include surgical trauma, malignant infiltration, and neuropathy, with a proportion remaining idiopathic. Loss of adductor and abductor tone leaves the fold in a paramedian or intermediate position. In unilateral loss the mobile fold cannot fully compensate, giving incomplete closure with a breathy voice and aspiration; in bilateral loss both folds sit near the midline, so the voice may be preserved but the airway is critically narrowed.
additionalDifferentials: Cricoarytenoid joint fixation (e.g. from rheumatoid arthritis or intubation trauma)
Central neurological disease affecting vagal nuclei
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy to confirm impaired mobility and fold position
Laryngeal electromyography to distinguish neurogenic paralysis from mechanical fixation and assess prognosis
CT from skull base to mediastinum to trace the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve course
Videostroboscopy to assess glottic closure and the mucosal wave
Targeted investigation for thyroid, oesophageal, pulmonary, or mediastinal pathology when no surgical cause is evident
redFlags: Bilateral paralysis with stridor or dyspnoea, an airway emergency
A new paralysis without an obvious surgical cause, mandating a search for malignancy along the nerve
Significant aspiration with recurrent chest infection or weight loss
Accompanying cranial nerve deficits pointing to a skull base or brainstem lesion
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic and some postsurgical unilateral palsies may recover over many months, and most patients achieve a functional voice with therapy or medialisation; bilateral paralysis has a more guarded outlook because improving the airway usually comes at the expense of voice quality.
pitfalls: Labelling a paralysis idiopathic before adequately imaging the entire course of the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve
Mistaking cricoarytenoid joint fixation for neurogenic paralysis without electromyography
Performing a permanent static medialisation too early, before spontaneous recovery has been given time
Underestimating the airway risk of bilateral paralysis and delaying airway protection
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Establish and treat the cause along the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve course, addressing any malignancy or thoracic pathology
Voice therapy for unilateral paralysis to aid compensation and improve glottic closure
Injection augmentation or medialisation thyroplasty, with arytenoid adduction where needed, when compensation is inadequate
Swallowing assessment and aspiration precautions because of poor glottic closure and weak cough
Prioritise the airway in bilateral paralysis, using acute tracheostomy then posterior cordotomy, arytenoidectomy or reinnervation to balance airway and voice
Laryngeal electromyography to assess prognosis and timing before permanent surgery
ENT laryngology and speech therapy referral
